g.title: Present simple and continuous; action and non-action verbs
g.rule:
Choose the tense by asking: is it always true / a habit, or is it happening now / temporary?

habits and facts → present simpleI usually cook at home. · She doesn't eat meat.
now or temporary → present continuousI'm cooking dinner now. · He's eating less sugar this month.
non-action verbs (like, know, want, need, prefer) → simple onlyI want a coffee. I'm wanting

Some verbs change meaning: I have two brothers (possess) but I'm having lunch (action).

ex.q: My sister ___ fish. She never eats it.
Be quiet, please. I ___ to the recipe.
This soup ___ delicious!
We ___ (not / usually / eat) out during the week.

talk: What do you usually eat on a normal weekday?
Are you trying to change anything about your diet at the moment?

r.text:
In many families Sunday lunch is the most important meal of the week, but it looks very different from house to house.

At Saule's home, lunch always means lamb. Her mother roasts it slowly with garlic and serves it with boiled potatoes and a fresh cucumber salad. "We never eat frozen food on Sunday," Saule says.

Her neighbour Tom prefers something quicker. He usually grills salmon and steams some cabbage. This month, however, he is trying to cut down on meat and fish, so he is experimenting with spicy vegetable dishes.

Across the road, the Kim family are eating raw fish and squid with rice. Their children, who are learning to cook, are making a raspberry dessert.

Three kitchens, three menus. But everybody agrees on one thing: the best meal is the one you share.

ex.q: What does Saule's family always eat on Sunday?
Tom is eating more meat this month.
What are the Kim children making?
What do all three families agree on?
o: The best meal is a shared one

g.title: Future forms: be going to, present continuous, will
g.rule:
English has no single future tense. Choose the form by the kind of future.

a plan or intention → be going toI'm going to visit my grandparents this summer.
a fixed arrangement (time, place) → present continuousWe're meeting my cousins at six.
a decision now, an offer, a promise, a prediction → willI'll help you. · I think he'll be a good father.

Use be going to for a prediction you can see: Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.

r.text:
Aruzhan lives in a flat with eight other people: her parents, two siblings, her grandparents, her great-grandmother and a baby cousin. "People think an extended family is noisy," she says. "They are right."

Everyone has a role. Her grandmother, who is affectionate but bossy, organises the kitchen. Her brother is the rebellious one, and her little sister can be moody. Aruzhan describes herself as reliable, although her mother says she is stubborn.

Next year things are going to change. Her brother is getting married in May, and the couple are moving to another city. Aruzhan is going to study abroad. "I think I'll miss the noise," she says. "My room there will be very quiet. I'll probably call home every day."

Her great-grandmother is not worried. "They'll come back," she says. "Families always do."

g.title: Present perfect and past simple
g.rule:
Both talk about the past. The question is: do we say when?

experience or news, no time given → present perfectI've bought a new phone. · Have you ever lent money to a friend?
a finished time (yesterday, last year, in 2020) → past simpleI bought it last week. It cost a lot.
just / already / yet → present perfectShe's already paid. · I haven't saved enough yet.

Conversations often start in the present perfect and continue in the past simple: “Have you ever wasted money?” “Yes, I bought a guitar and never played it.”

ex.q: I ___ my wallet yesterday.
___ you ever ___ anything online and regretted it?

r.text:
Have you ever looked at your bank account and wondered where your money went? Last January, 26-year-old designer Madina decided to find out.

For thirty days she paid only for rent, bills and basic food. She didn't buy coffee, clothes or taxis, and she didn't borrow anything. "The first week was awful," she says. "I've never felt so bored."

By the end of the month, however, she had saved more than she usually saved in half a year. She has also changed some habits. She has cancelled two subscriptions she never used, and she has started taking lunch to work.

Not everything worked. She has already bought the shoes she wanted in January. "But I've learned something useful," she says. "I can afford most things. I just can't afford everything."

g.title: Present perfect + for / since; present perfect continuous
g.rule:
Use these forms for something that started in the past and is still true now.

for + a period · since + a starting pointI've lived here for three years / since 2022.
action verbs → present perfect continuous (have been + -ing)She's been working for a charity since May.
non-action verbs (know, be, have) → present perfect simpleWe've known each other for ages.

The continuous form is also used for a recent activity with a visible result: You look tired. Have you been running?

talk: What have you been doing recently that is new for you?

r.text:
Three years ago Bolat could not run for a bus. He was working twelve hours a day and felt exhausted all the time. Then a friend asked him to join a short charity run.

"I was terrified," he remembers. "I finished last, I was starving and my legs were shaking. But I was also delighted."

Since then he has been running four times a week. He has completed twelve marathons and has been raising money for a children's hospital for two years. So far his sponsors have given more than five million tenge.

His doctor is amazed. Bolat has lost fifteen kilos, and he has been sleeping better than at any time since his twenties.

His next goal is huge: sixty marathons before he turns sixty. "I've known for a long time that I'm not fast," he says. "But I've discovered that I don't stop."

Every country has laws, but good manners are different: nobody writes them down. Phones have created a whole new set of them.

Most people agree on the basics. You should put your phone on silent mode in a cinema, and you mustn't answer a call during a job interview. You don't have to reply to every message immediately, although some friends seem to think you do.

Other situations are less clear. Should you send a voice note or write? Many people over forty say you should always ask before you call. Many teenagers say you shouldn't call at all.

Restaurants are starting to make their own rules. One café in the city centre says customers have to leave their phones in a basket at the door. In return, they don't have to pay for their first coffee.

r.text:
A two-hour film can take three years to make, and most of the work is never seen by the audience.

First, the script is written and rewritten, sometimes twenty times. Then the cast is chosen. Famous stars are often contacted before the script has even been finished, because their names help to find money.

After filming, the soundtrack is recorded and the film is cut. Whole scenes are often removed. Finally, a trailer is made, and the film is dubbed or given subtitles for other countries.

r.text:
Can you tell what a stranger is feeling from a photograph? Most of us think we can, and most of us are sometimes wrong.

Look at a person with wide eyes and an open mouth. She might be frightened, but she could also be surprised, or she may simply be singing. Without the rest of the picture we can't be sure. A man who is staring at the floor might be sad. Then again, he might have dropped his keys.

Psychologists say we look at the whole body, not only the face. Somebody whose shoulders are up near their ears must be tense. A person who nods and smiles while pointing their feet at the door can't be enjoying the conversation very much.

So the next time you are certain that somebody is angry with you, remember: they might just need new glasses.

talk: Tell us about a time you complained in a shop or restaurant. What did they say?

r.text:
Last spring Timur ordered a sofa online. The website said it would arrive in two weeks. Six weeks later he was still sitting on the floor.

He phoned the company. The assistant told him that the sofa was on its way and said she would call him back. She didn't. A week later a different assistant said that there had been a problem at the factory and asked him if he could wait another month.

Timur decided to write instead. In his email he explained what had happened, said how long he had waited, and asked politely for a refund or a delivery date. He told them that he would post a review if he did not get a response in five days.

The manager replied the next morning. She apologised, said that the service had been unacceptable, and offered him compensation. The sofa arrived that Friday.

His advice? "Be polite, be clear, and put it in writing."

r.text:
People often say that small things change our lives. For Aigerim, it was a broken alarm clock.

Ten years ago she was travelling to a job interview in another city. Her alarm didn't ring, and she missed her train by two minutes. "If I had caught it, I would have arrived on time," she says. "And I probably would have got the job."

Instead she waited three hours at the station. A woman sat down next to her and they started talking. The stranger was opening a language school and needed a manager.

"If my alarm had worked, I wouldn't have met her," Aigerim says. "I wouldn't have changed my career, and I would never have moved here."

Does she believe in luck? "Not exactly. If I hadn't talked to her, nothing would have happened. You can't choose your chances, but you can choose to take them."

r.text:
On Friday evening a storm cut the electricity in our street. It did not come back until Monday.

At first there was too much silence. There was no television, no music and no Wi-Fi. My brother had very little battery on his phone, and none of us had any cash, because we pay for everything by card.

We found a few candles and plenty of blankets. There wasn't enough hot food, so we ate a lot of bread and cheese. We played cards, and my father told several stories that I had never heard.

On Sunday a neighbour who has a small generator invited everybody in the building to charge their phones. Too many people came, and not enough of them brought a charger.

When the lights came on, we all cheered. Then, one by one, we picked up our screens. I spent too much time on mine that evening. I had missed it, and I was a little sorry that I had.

talk: Describe a person you admire: who are they, and what have they done?

r.text:
Every country has people whose faces everybody recognises. But what makes a person an icon?

Some are admired for a single achievement. The first astronaut, who spent less than two hours in space, became a hero for millions of people who had never met him.

Others are remembered for a whole career. A scientist whose discovery saved thousands of lives may be less famous than a singer, which seems unfair to many people.

Then there are the icons that are not people at all: a red phone box, a yellow taxi, a tower where tourists queue for hours. These are objects which were designed for everyday use and which later became symbols.

Perhaps the most interesting icons are the ones we choose ourselves. Ask a teenager who they admire, and the answer is often a teacher, a coach or a grandmother, somebody whose name will never be on a banknote.

o: A scientist may be less famous than a singer

ex.q: All icons are people.

o: A teacher, a coach or a grandmother

r.text:
The Central Museum had only one famous painting, and on a Monday morning in March it was gone.

Inspector Akhmetov arrived at nine. "The alarm didn't ring, did it?" he asked the director.

"No. It was switched off at midnight."

"And only three people know the code, don't they?"

"Yes. Myself, the guard and the cleaner."

The guard said he had been asleep. The cleaner said she had left at ten. The inspector looked at the floor near the empty wall. There was a little water on it.

"It wasn't raining last night, was it?" he said. "But the garden is watered at one o'clock." He turned to the director. "You came in through the garden door, didn't you? Your shoes are still wet."

The director said nothing. The painting was found in his car an hour later. He had needed money, he explained, and nobody ever suspects the victim.
